$comment:
Maximum findings each rule may report across the pinned corpus in scripts/corpus-scan.ts, measured against the PUBLISHED plugin versions — the ones in each package.json, which is what a consumer installing today gets. A fix landing on main does NOT move these numbers until it is released, and that is deliberate: this gate reports shipped behaviour, not intent.

This is a RATCHET: lower an entry whenever the scan reports a rule under budget, which will typically be the release after the fix. Raising an entry requires `npx tsx scripts/corpus-scan.ts --update` so the increase is reviewable and deliberate. A rule absent from this file is budgeted at 0, so a newly-noisy rule cannot arrive unnoticed.

triage.browser-security/no-eval: okta-signin-widget scripts/buildtools/commands/generate-phone-codes.js: axios.get(METADATA_URI).then(({data}) => { ... eval(data) }). Evaluating a payload fetched over the network — the strongest true positive in this batch. A build script, so it is their risk to accept, but the rule is exactly right.
triage.browser-security/no-unencrypted-transmis: ioredis lib/utils/index.ts: `new URL('redis://' + rawUrl)` — a dummy scheme prepended so URL() can parse a protocol-less host:port, per the target's own comment. Nothing is transmitted. The rule deliberately OWNS redis:// (no other rule covers the non-web cleartext protocols) and matches the scheme wherever it appears, including `new URLSearchParams`. Exempting URL parsers was considered and rejected: `const u = new URL('redis://host'); client.connect(u)` would then go silent, because the connect site carries no literal. Budgeted rather than narrowed — a recall loss is the worse trade for a security rule.
triage.node-security/no-toctou-vulnerability: okta-auth-js rollup.config.js: `if (!existsSync(d)) mkdirSync(d, {recursive:true})`. NOT a false positive. An exemption was written and reverted: with recursive:true an attacker who plants a symlink in the window gets mkdir to succeed SILENTLY and later writes follow it, where plain mkdir throws EEXIST and the program notices. The flag makes the race worse. Budgeted because the finding is correct and the target is a build script we do not control.
triage.node-security/require-dependency-integri: Shopify/cli, three HTML template literals that pull Polaris and graphiql CSS from jsdelivr and unpkg with no integrity= attribute. All three are correct SRI findings. Note error-page.ts: my own grep for external URLs MISSED it because the href is an interpolated constant (${POLARIS_STYLESHEET_URL}); the rule saw it and I did not.
triage.secure-coding/no-redos-vulnerable-regex:
7 -> 5 -> 7. REVERSED. The ratchet to 5 came from asking the oracle for the DEGREE rather than only whether the pattern is vulnerable at all, and then defaulting degree 2 off. Two of those findings are quadratic over short, sized input (^###\s+(.+)$ over one markdown heading) and nobody would act on them, so under Google's effective-FP standard the ratchet looked right.

The CWE-1333 recall gate rejected it. benchmarks/corpus/CWE-1333/vulnerable/trade-off.js pins /^(a*).*b/ as must-detect and recheck scores it degree 2, so the default dropped a detection. Degree only PROXIES the question that decides actionability — does the caller size the input — and nothing in the AST answers it. When the proxy and the calibrated corpus disagree, a security rule keeps the finding. Default flipped back to reporting; the quieter bar is opt-in via reportSecondDegreePolynomial: false and costs recall by construction.

So 2 of these 7 are known effective FPs, recorded rather than hidden. Buying them off with a default that costs a true positive was the wrong trade; the real fix is a bounded-input signal, which does not exist yet.

What DID survive: the rig now installs recheck. It never had, and recheck is an optional peer whose absence makes confirmsRedos fail open, so every ReDoS number recorded here before 2026-08-20 was measured with the oracle switched off. Installing it changed the count by zero — all 7 are oracle-confirmed.
triage.secure-coding/no-sensitive-data-exposure:
6 -> 2, ratcheted DOWN. Both survivors are REAL and neither should be silenced: Shopify bin/github-utils.js:37 `console.log(`Using token from ${source}: ${tokenFromEnv}`)` and :43 `console.log(`Using password from dev: ${password}`)` log an actual credential value.

The four that went away were one shape: the static PROSE names a credential while every interpolated VALUE names itself an outcome — twilio TokenAuthStrategy.ts:22, ApiTokenManager.ts:36, OrgsTokenManager.ts:36 (`Failed to fetch access token: ${error.message}`, `Error Status Code: ${error.status}`) and Shopify graphiql-token-provider.ts:38 (`Token request failed with status ${tokenResponse.status}`). The label describes the operation that FAILED; the property says what is actually printed. Property is structure, prose is not, so the property wins.

Two report paths had to be closed, not one. The text heuristic fired on label-separator-hole, and the VALUE path fired separately on `tokenResponse.status` by reading the RECEIVER's name and ignoring what was taken from it — the same defect VALUE_FREE_PROPERTIES already fixed for `.length`, one property set over. DIAGNOSTIC_ACCESSORS (message, stack, name, status, statusText) is protocol-grounded the same way: Error.prototype and the Fetch response, not vocabulary. `code` is deliberately excluded — an authorization code, a 2FA code and a recovery code are all called `code`.

Recall unchanged: CWE corpus 69/69, FP=0. Six FN guards pin the two real corpus leaks, an opaque hole under the same label, a mixed template, `code`, and a computed read.
triage.node-security/require-stream-error-handl:
4, and all 4 are TRUE POSITIVES. Re-examined 2026-08-21 because 'there is an error handler three lines up' made them look like obvious FPs. They are not, and the question is always WHICH STREAM the handler is attached to:

Shopify archiver.ts:55 and :163 blame `output`, the write stream. `archive.on('error')` covers the archiver; `output` has only an 'close' listener, so a disk-full or EACCES on the destination is an uncaught exception. .pipe() does not forward errors in either direction.

okta ImageDiff.js:12 blames `fs.createReadStream(image)`. The chained `.on('error', reject)` attaches to the PNG DESTINATION, not the source, so ENOENT on a missing image is unhandled — the classic pipe gotcha the rule exists for.

okta ImageDiff.js:63 has no handler on either end at all.

Do not 'fix' this rule by treating a nearby .on('error') as coverage. Any such change must keep these four reporting.
triage.node-security/no-unsafe-buffer-alloc:
3, all `new Array(length)` in redis/ioredis lib/resp/decoder.ts (669, 735, 803). Kept. `length` is the RESP wire length prefix, so it is decided by the server on the other end of the socket, and the rule's own measured note explains why this shape matters: the cost is a narrow band below V8's packed-elements limit (~33.5M), where 12 wire bytes buy 229 MB, rather than a monotonic function of n.

Weaker threat model than a public HTTP input — it takes a compromised or MITM'd Redis server — which is why these are budgeted rather than treated as must-fix. Not silenced: the rationale is measured and written down, and `new Array` is in SIZED_ALLOCATORS on purpose.
triage.reliability/no-missing-null-checks:
38,674 -> 127. Batch 1. The rule's model was INVERTED, not tuned.

It reported every member expression whose object could not be PROVEN non-null, which on real source is very nearly every property access. The rule's own notes had measured the same thing from the other end — 'this rule alone was 56% of everything recommended reports across all 30 plugins' — and answered it by growing the deny-list, which cannot converge: the set of things that are never null is unbounded without types.

A finding now needs POSITIVE evidence: `let x;` never written, `= null` / `= undefined`, or a platform-documented nullable return (find, findLast, pop, shift, match, exec, getElementById, querySelector, closest, getAttribute). `.get` is deliberately excluded — Map.get really is nullable but axios.get, router.get and cache.get are far more common.

Two bugs found on the way down, both mine: a `for…of` head is a VariableDeclarator with a null init and was read as `let x;` (668 -> 429), and `let x` written later is deferred initialisation, not a read of undefined (429 -> 127).

One bug found that was NOT mine: `hasNullCheck` used `leftText.endsWith(objectText)`, so in `wrapper.obj && obj.prop` the guard on `wrapper.obj` suppressed the finding on `obj`. The test meant to catch it passed for the wrong reason — its single expected error came from `wrapper.obj` itself under the old model.

The 127 remaining are spot-checked true positives: unchecked `.match()` results indexed directly, `.find()` results dereferenced. okta-auth-js writes `remediationChoiceObject.action!` and `remediation.value!` at two of them — the codebase already uses non-null assertions to silence TypeScript about exactly this.

Budget 127 -> 139, an INCREASE and a deliberate one. Positioning the write check against the read recovered `let m = null; const hooks = m.hooks; m = result.m` — a read of null that a later reassignment had been excusing. Twelve such reads exist on the pinned corpus.
triage.reliability/require-network-timeout: 40. Kept. `await fetch(url)` with no AbortSignal or timeout. Node's fetch has NO default timeout, so a hung connection hangs the caller forever — this is the rule's contract and the findings are in it. Sampled Shopify/cli: create-homebrew-pr.js:138/152, get-graphql-schemas.js:124, bundle.ts:70, graphiql-token-provider.ts:26. Weaker case in one-shot bin/ scripts than in the shipped CLI, which is why it is budgeted rather than must-fix.
triage.reliability/no-silent-errors: 36. Kept. Literal `catch (error) {}` and bare `catch {}` with an empty body — a swallowed failure with nothing logged and nothing rethrown. Sampled Shopify/cli: create-test-app.js:92, create-test-theme.js:88, update-observe.js:395/417, public_metadata.ts:20, loader.ts:325. In contract and defensible; budgeted because an empty catch in a metrics hook is a deliberate choice a maintainer would not act on.
triage.browser-security/no-credentials-in-query: 1. okta-signin-widget src/v1/util/RouterUtil.js:34 — a handlebars template `{{baseUrl}}/login/sessionCookieRedirect?...&token={{{token}}}`. CORRECT: a session token in a query string is CWE-598, and query strings reach logs, proxies and Referer headers. Budgeted rather than must-fix because the URL shape is Okta's own published API contract — the maintainer cannot change it from this file.
triage.browser-security/no-innerhtml: 3, all okta-signin-widget: FormInputFactory.ts:19, EndUserRemediationMessageViewUtil.js:78, probeLoopbackAndExecute.ts:60. Writes to innerHTML in a widget that renders server-supplied remediation content — squarely the rule's contract. Budgeted, not silenced.
triage.browser-security/no-unsafe-inline-csp: 1. okta-signin-widget Gruntfile.js:267 — a `script-src` string containing an inline allowance. CORRECT reading of the directive; it is BUILD tooling rather than shipped policy, which is why it is budgeted.
triage.browser-security/require-blob-url-revoca: 1. okta-signin-widget src/util/Altcha.ts:47 — a createObjectURL with no matching revokeObjectURL on the same path. A leaked blob URL pins its buffer for the document's lifetime; correct and in contract.
triage.node-security/detect-eval-with-expressio: 1. okta-signin-widget scripts/buildtools/commands/generate-phone-codes.js:20 — `eval(data)` where `data` came off a network fetch. Batch 0 called this the strongest true positive on the corpus. Build-time script, so budgeted rather than must-fix; the same line is also reported by browser-security/no-eval, which is the two plugins' documented overlap, not a duplicate.
triage.node-security/detect-non-literal-fs-file: 2. Shopify/cli bin/update-bugsnag.js:33 and :36 — a temp path built at runtime and passed to fs.cpSync. Correct: the argument is not a literal. A release script the maintainer controls end to end, hence budgeted.
triage.node-security/no-math-random-crypto: 1. okta-auth-js lib/util/misc.ts:25 — Math.random() in a value that feeds identifier generation. Correct: Math.random is not a CSPRNG. Budgeted because the value is a nonce-ish string rather than a key or token.
triage.node-security/no-shell-injection: 1. Shopify/cli packages/plugin-cloudflare/src/install-cloudflared.ts:135 — `execSync(`t...`)` with an interpolated template. Correct shape for the rule; the interpolated value is an install path the CLI itself computes.
triage.node-security/no-unsafe-dynamic-require: 1. okta-signin-widget src/v3/src/mocks/browser.ts:34 — a require with a computed specifier in a MOCK harness. Correct shape, test-support file.
triage.secure-coding/no-graphql-injection: 1. Shopify/cli .../graphql/organization_beta_flags.ts:4 — TRUE POSITIVE and the strongest finding in this group. `flags.map(f => `flag_${f}: hasFeatureFlag(handle: "${f}")`)` interpolates straight into the query body AND inside a quoted GraphQL string, so a `"` in a flag name breaks out. Budgeted only because the flag list is internal; it should be fixed upstream.
triage.secure-coding/no-unlimited-resource-allo: 1. Shopify/cli packages/app/src/cli/services/function/binaries.ts:315 — a gunzip stream with no size cap. Correct: a decompression bomb is bounded by nothing here. The archive is fetched from Shopify's own CDN, which is why it is budgeted.
triage.import-next/export:
778 -> 3. Batch 2, and a clear-cut RULE BUG. TypeScript has two declaration spaces and a name may occupy both:

  export type Twilio = ITwilio
  export const Twilio = ITwilio     // legal, and the point of the pattern

The rule kept ONE map keyed by name, so every such pair was 'Multiple exports of name X'. twilio-node's src/index.ts alone produced 758 of them. Fixed by splitting value space from type space, with `interface X` twice treated as declaration MERGING (legal) while `type X` twice, `type X` beside `interface X`, and an enum against either are still reported — an enum occupies both spaces. Six valid cases verified to FAIL against the old rule.
triage.import-next/order: 1825. Correct in contract — import groups genuinely out of order. LOW severity style, dominated by large generated SDK trees (okta-auth-js, twilio-node). Nobody reorders generated imports, so these are effective FPs under the Tricorder standard, but the rule is not wrong; the question is whether a style rule belongs in `recommended`, which is a preset decision rather than a rule defect.
triage.import-next/newline-after-import: 693. Correct in contract. Same class as `order` — LOW-severity formatting over generated files, where imports are interleaved with `const x = require(...)` so the 'last import' is genuinely ambiguous.
triage.import-next/first: 577. Correct in contract, and the finding is real: twilio-node's generated clients emit `import`, then `const deserialize = require(...)`, then more `import`s. An import after non-import statements is exactly what the rule is for. Generated code, so nobody acts.
triage.import-next/no-cycle: 1337. Correct — real circular imports, concentrated in generated SDK class hierarchies (twilio Page/Version/AccountsBase, okta idx remediators). CVSS 5.3 / CRITICAL is severity inflation for a circular import and is worth revisiting separately; the DETECTION is right.
triage.import-next/no-duplicates: 37. Correct — two import statements from the same module in one file.
triage.import-next/no-empty-named-blocks: 1. Correct — an `import {} from 'x'` with an empty named block.
triage.conventions/no-commented-code:
2,441 -> 143. Batch 3, and the FPs were English rather than code. Three mechanics inside `looksLikeCode`, all measured on the pinned corpus:

  `Copyright (c) 2018 …`   the call pattern allowed whitespace before `(`, so every legal banner in okta-auth-js reported
  `https://example.com/x`  matched the `ident:` assignment pattern — `https:` reads as a label — so every documentation link reported
  `for backward compat…`   a sentence that merely OPENS with a JavaScript keyword: 'for widget / idx-js backward compatibility', 'if no key is passed', 'let existing promise finish', 'return all cookies when…'

The discriminator that survived is punctuation. Commented-out code is COPIED out of a file and keeps its semicolons and braces; a sentence ends in a word. Known trade, recorded rather than hidden: a terminator-less fragment such as `// x = 1` is no longer reported.

A fourth fix was written and then DELETED — a special case for the terser `/*!` preserve banner. It was unreachable: tightening the paren pattern already covered every banner, and the guard only looked load-bearing.

The 143 remaining are real: `const target = actionDefinition.href;`, `err = wwwAuthErr ?? err;`, `const inputs = this.getInputs();` — commented-out bodies in okta-auth-js's generateIdxAction.ts and GenericRemediator.ts.

Budget 143 -> 91. The JSDoc exemption removed the `@example` bodies that were reporting as commented-out code.
triage.conventions/no-magic-numbers:
1635. Correct in contract, and a taste rule by nature. Sampled okta-auth-js: HTTP status codes (`err.xhr.status === 429`), millisecond timeouts (`15 * 1000`, `options?.timeout || 15000`), backoff arithmetic (`Math.pow(2, retryCount) * 1000`) and ESLint config tuples in `.eslintrc.js` (`complexity: [2, 7]`). The config-file case is the one worth revisiting — a config is declarative data rather than logic — but that is a scope decision for the rule, not a defect, so it is budgeted rather than changed here.

1,635 -> 1,421 on the pinned corpus; 22,942 -> 15,924 on the 20-repo ledger. Three exemptions, and the big one was NOT the one I predicted.

The gaps recorded here named loop bounds and arity checks as the dominant classes. I had inferred that from about a dozen sampled lines, and it was wrong: implementing both removed 178 findings out of 22,942. Measuring the distribution properly over 5,938 sampled findings gave a different answer — object property VALUES were 1,827 of them, 31% and the largest context by a factor of two, against 231 for if/while conditions and 79 for comparisons.

So `detectObjects` was added, defaulting to FALSE — which is what ESLint core's own no-magic-numbers has shipped for years. A config object is a place to write literals; that is what it is for. Matching the baseline everyone already expects is the whole change, and it accounts for the entire 31%.

`ignoreLoopBounds` and `ignoreLengthComparisons` are kept because they are correct, not because they were large. The length exemption is EQUALITY only: `arguments.length === 3` is an arity check, `users.length > 100` is a business threshold — an existing test pinned exactly that shape and it was right.

Still reported and still recorded as gaps: protocol constants (`status >= 400`, `port !== 27017`, character codes) and config FILES, neither of which can be told from an arbitrary number without knowing what is being compared.
triage.conventions/analytics-event-naming: 1. Correct in contract — a single analytics event name off the configured taxonomy.
triage.maintainability/identical-functions:
3,530 -> 2,075. Batch 4. THREE bugs in `normalizeBody`, each erasing something that distinguishes one function from another:

1. KEYWORDS. The rename pattern `[a-z_$][a-zA-Z0-9_$]*` matches `return`, `throw`, `if` and `this` as well as bindings, so `return VAR.VAR(VAR)` and `throw VAR.VAR(VAR)` were the same string. Once bindings are generic, control flow is the ONLY thing left to compare, and it was being erased — every function sharing a bracket shape became a duplicate.

2. COMMENTS ran LAST, after `\s+` had collapsed the body onto one line. At that point `//.*` matches from the first line comment to the END of the function and deletes the rest of it, so two bodies were compared as their opening lines. Moved ahead of the whitespace collapse.

3. STRING CONTENTS were renamed too, so `"/api/v1/authn/recovery/password"` and `"/api/v1/authn/recovery/unlock"` both became `"/VAR/VAR/VAR/VAR/VAR"` and two methods calling different endpoints compared 100% identical.

Property names are now kept for the same reason — `.create(x)` and `.destroy(x)` are not one call.

Three more were found in review on #595 — comment removal matched the `//` inside "https://…" and deleted the rest of the FUNCTION; unquoted object KEYS were renamed, so { create: id } and { destroy: id } were one string; and `async`/`*` live on the NODE rather than in node.body, so an async function and its synchronous twin matched. String literals are now lifted out before anything else touches the text, keys are preserved like property names, and the modifiers are compared as a GATE rather than folded into the text — a 2-character `* ` prefix still leaves two bodies 95% similar.

The 2,075 that remain are real, and concentrated: 1,643 in twilio-node, a GENERATED SDK whose CRUD methods are near-identical by construction, 115 in Shopify/cli, 41 in okta-auth-js. Correct detections that nobody would act on, because refactoring generated code is not a thing — effective FPs under the Tricorder standard, but not rule defects.

Note on the threshold, since it looks like a bug and is not: `/api/v1/authn/recovery/password` vs `.../unlock` drops from 100% to exactly 90% once contents are preserved, which is the DEFAULT threshold. That pair still reports, correctly.

Budget correction: 2,075 -> 2,076. The 2,075 was measured BEFORE the last fix on this branch (regex and multiline-template protection) and I set the budget from it without re-running. CI caught the one-finding gap. Protecting those two literal forms preserves more text, which shifts which functions group with which, and a group boundary moving changes the count by one — benign, but the measurement was stale, not the rule. Same trap as `fix-verified-against-a-reduction`: re-measure after the LAST change, not after the one you were thinking about.

Budget 2,076 -> 1,631. Requiring an EXACT match below 120 normalised characters removed the pairs differing by a single load-bearing token.
triage.maintainability/cognitive-complexity: 671. Correct in contract — functions over the configured cognitive-complexity budget, concentrated in generated SDK dispatch and in okta's idx remediator tree. A measurement of the target's code, not a defect in ours.
triage.maintainability/max-parameters: 185. Correct in contract — functions over the configured parameter count. Same character as cognitive-complexity: a true statement about the target.
triage.modularity/ddd-anemic-domain-model:
526. Batch 5, and the largest entry in it. Correct in contract: the rule flags classes that hold data without behaviour. Sampled okta-auth-js — AuthnTransactionImpl, OktaAuthBase, BaseOptionsConstructor — and every one is a transport or options object in an SDK, which is exactly what an anemic model looks like and exactly what an SDK is supposed to ship.

A philosophical mismatch rather than a defect: DDD is an opinion about DOMAIN code, and it is being applied to a client library. Budgeted. Whether this rule belongs in `recommended` is a preset question of the same kind raised by the style rules in Batch 2.
triage.modernization/prefer-template-literal: 185. Correct — `'okta-auth-js/' + SDK_VERSION`, `sdk.getIssuerOrigin() + '/api/v1/authn'`. String concatenation that reads better as a template. LOW-value style, no defect.
triage.operability/no-debug-code-in-production: 120. Correct detection, wrong audience. Sampled okta-auth-js: env/index.js:22 and scripts/verify-package.js:3 — `console.log` in BUILD scripts and env loaders, not shipped code. The rule is right that it is debug output; the gap is that a repo's `scripts/`, `bin/` and `env/` trees are not production. Worth a path-scoping option, which is a scope decision rather than a bug.
triage.modularity/ddd-value-object-immutability: 11. Correct — value-object fields reassigned after construction.
triage.modularity/enforce-rest-conventions: 6. Correct — route shapes off the configured REST convention.
triage.modularity/no-external-api-calls-in-util: 1. Correct — a network call from a util module.
triage.modularity/no-mutable-exports: 1. Correct — an exported binding that is reassigned.
triage.modernization/prefer-event-target: 17. Correct — Node EventEmitter where the cross-platform EventTarget would do.
triage.modernization/no-instanceof-array: 1. Correct — `instanceof Array` fails across realms; `Array.isArray` does not.
triage.operability/no-console-log:
107. Correct, and deliberately overlapping with operability/no-debug-code-in-production (120) — the two report the same `console.log` lines under different framings, one as 'do not log from a library', the other as 'this is debug code'. Sampled okta-auth-js env/index.js:22 and scripts/verify-package.js:3/:12: build scripts and env loaders, not shipped code.

Same gap as its twin: a repo's `scripts/`, `bin/` and `env/` trees are not production, and neither rule scopes by path. Worth one shared path-scoping option rather than two; that is a scope decision, not a defect. The overlap is also worth a partition note — two rules reporting one line is the shape the browser-security URL family was already partitioned to avoid.
triage.react-features/hooks-exhaustive-deps:
91. Correct in contract — a hook dependency array missing a value the effect reads. The canonical React correctness rule; a missing dep is a stale-closure bug, not a style opinion.

Measurement note — budgeted at 91, the MAXIMUM observed, and the mechanism is still unknown.

What is established: CI itself has read BOTH 84 and 91, on different runs of the same corpus. This machine reads 84 every time — three consecutive scans, a direct per-repo count (okta-signin-widget 46 + Shopify/cli 38, identical finding sets by sha1 across three runs each), and every other target zero.

What has been ruled OUT, each by measurement rather than argument:
  - plugin staleness. It persists with the rig installing PUBLISHED, immutable versions, so there is no local build to go stale.
  - the `file:` npm cache. Same reason.
  - filesystem case-sensitivity between macOS and Linux. `git ls-files` case-folded shows no colliding paths in either react-heavy target.

So the budget is the maximum, because a gate that fails on a coin flip is worse than one budgeted 7 findings loose. This is the ONE number here that is not a measurement of the rules, and it is labelled as such rather than quietly rounded.

My own handling of it is recorded because the reasoning was the failure: I called 84 the truth, corrected to 91 arguing CI is authoritative, corrected back when CI read 84, and am now back at 91 with better evidence and less confidence. The lesson is not which number — it is that I kept asserting one while the instrument was visibly disagreeing with itself.
triage.react-features/no-unknown-property: 65. Correct — DOM props spelled the HTML way rather than the React way (`class`, `for`, `tabindex`). Concentrated in okta-signin-widget's older JSX.
triage.react-a11y/prefer-tag-over-role: 31. Correct — `<div role="button">` where `<button>` carries the semantics, focus and keyboard behaviour for free.
triage.react-features/jsx-key: 13. Correct — a list element rendered without a key. A real reconciliation bug.
triage.react-a11y/click-events-have-key-events: 7. Correct — onClick with no keyboard equivalent, so the control is mouse-only.
triage.react-a11y/interactive-supports-focus: 7. Correct — an interactive element that cannot be reached by keyboard.
triage.react-features/no-children-prop: 2. Correct — `children` passed as a prop rather than nested.
triage.react-a11y/iframe-has-title: 1. Correct — an iframe with no accessible name.
triage.__measurement__:
2026-08-22: the rig stopped installing the plugins as local `file:` dependencies and now installs the PUBLISHED versions.

Why it matters for reading every number here: a `file:` dependency is served from npm's cache when its version has not changed, so the rig kept measuring a PREVIOUS local build. That cost most of a day — no-magic-numbers read 1,635 against a fresh 1,421 with no ratchet notice at all, and hooks-exhaustive-deps read both 84 and 91 across clean CI runs. A published version is immutable, so the same version string is always the same code and the class of bug is gone rather than mitigated.

The consequence, stated plainly: four budgets went UP when this landed — identical-functions 1,631 -> 2,076, no-magic-numbers 1,421 -> 1,635, no-commented-code 91 -> 143 — and one went DOWN, no-missing-null-checks 139 -> 127. Those are not regressions. They are today's fixes not being released yet, and the null-checks one is a detection IMPROVEMENT that has not shipped either. Each should ratchet to the fixed value at the next release.
triage.import-next/no-extraneous-dependencies: UNADJUDICATED. This rule was excluded as unmeasurable and never belonged in that set — it compares imports against package.json, not against the installed tree, and reports identically before and after an install. The budget is the first measurement, not a verdict. Read on auth0/express-openid-connect, 10 findings: 5 are TRUE (@eslint/js, globals and body-parser are used and undeclared, arriving transitively), and 5 are FALSE — `require('..')` and `import from '.'` are relative self-references, not dependencies, and the rule counts them. Fixing that is the next batch item and will ratchet this down.
